This haiku exemplifies modern Japanese poetry's departure from Bashō-esque nature reverence toward urban existentialism, akin to Shiki's shasei (sketching from life) but infused with postwar disillusion (echoing Hagiwara Sakutaro's sensory fragmentation). A masterful anti-haiku, it subverts seasonal kigo (spring thunder as faux-renewal) to expose affection's inherent betrayal, rewarding rereads with deepening cynicism.
